title: Delta Air Lines Even Owns An Oil Refinery And Claimed To Be Carbon Neutral
description:
Delta’s Carbon Neutrality Claims Were Based On Bogus Offsets Delta announced in February 2020 that it would spend $1 billion over ten years and become carbon neutral on March 1.
It turns out to be ripe for fraud and Delta’s credits in particular turned out to be highly problematic.
The Sham Carbon Credits Became National News Delta used to brag about its involvement with the Kariba project in Zimbabwe.
But bad for the people hawking carbon credits.
Delta Probably Prevails Delta made an absolute claim about current carbon neutrality and relied on a voluntary market with real weaknesses to deliver on the claim.
text:
A federal judge ruled that a passenger pursuing a class action lawsuit against Delta Air Lines can keep pursuing damages after it purported to be “the world’s first carbon-neutral airline,” even though they’re a fossil-fuel burning carrier with an aging fleet, own an oil refinery (and interest in a private jet company), and the claims turn out not to be true. The court rejected Delta’s the latest effort to end the case over its bogus environmental claims.

Companies were leaning into ESG in 2020. Greenwashing was de rigueur. But this lawsuit fascinates me because it raises the question of whether it was all just marketing puffery, or if there’s real liability for claims that don’t come true? And why is it that airlines get a legal get out of jail free card on this?

U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong’s July 28, 2026 ruling lets the plaintiff try to prove that Delta violated California’s Consumers Legal Remedies Act. They didn’t get an injunction, though, because Delta stopped promoting they were carbon-neutral on March 31, 2022, and the lead plaintiff acknowledged understanding Delta’s current marketing goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.

The original lawsuit was filed on May 30, 2023 and here’s the third amended complaint.

Delta’s Carbon Neutrality Claims Were Based On Bogus Offsets

Delta announced in February 2020 that it would spend $1 billion over ten years and become carbon neutral on March 1. The message was that Delta had “become the first carbon neutral airline on a global basis” and had been “carbon neutral since March 2020.” This was in press releases, social media, a podcast, Delta.com banners, a paid campaign, seatback screens and an in-flight napkin.

As flights continued burning jet fuel, Delta treated emissions reductions purchased elsewhere as balancing that fuel burn, with the complaint describing plans to spend more than $30 million on credits for about 13 million metric tons of 2020 emissions and Delta saying it ultimately spent more than $280 million on credits from March 2020 through March 2022. Much of that money was apparently wasted.

I was skeptical when Delta announced carbon neutrality in 2020 because carbon credits rely on assumptions about events that never occur (how much deforestation might happen without paying someone not to chop down trees). It turns out to be ripe for fraud and Delta’s credits in particular turned out to be highly problematic.

Delta added canned wine, bamboo cutlery and recycled polyester bedding to its environmental story in a 2022 “eco-conscious” amenities announcement.

A carbon credit project promises to preserve a forest. The credit has value if the trees faced a real threat, the payment caused the protection, and nobody else claims the same reduction. Each credit depends on a counterfactual claim about the world where that specific credit was never purchased.

The lawsuit is over the credits in Delta’s portfolio including funky accounting, preservation projects that would have proceeded anyway, delayed reductions in emissions and double counting.

The Sham Carbon Credits Became National News

Delta used to brag about its involvement with the Kariba project in Zimbabwe. Bloomberg‘s Matt Levine calls the folks involved “ESG Consultant[s] But Evil.”

As Levine explains, “(1) the money kind of disappeared and (2) a lot of the carbon credits turned out to be fake.” The New Yorker‘s Heidi Blake has the owner of the forest generating the credits on the record, “I don’t know what you’re going to report on this, and I hope to God it’s not all of it, because I probably will go to jail.”

It turns out that they sort of made up numbers as a benchmark for how much deforestation would have happened without a forest’s preservation. There was a reference forest nearby and it basically showed not so much deforestation was happening without the preservations. So the credits weren’t really protecting forests. And they oversold the credits (effectively selling the same fake credits to multiple buyers). Matt Levine:

The problem with this anti-deforestation project was that there was too little deforestation. That seems good? For the climate? But bad for the people hawking carbon credits. The idealistic Muench pointed out the problem, and the now-jaded Heuberger was like “meh still fine”:

Is There A Strong Case For Damages?

California law bars a business from misrepresenting the characteristics, benefits or quality of a service. A key question is whether anyone bought Delta tickets, or paid more to fly Delta, because they were deceived about Delta’s eco-consciousness.

Delta argued that the Airline Deregulation Act preempts the case because state law can’t regulate airline rates and services. The judge rejected that argument because California left Delta free to choose its environmental program, and treated carbon offsets as investments separate from the flight itself.

This is going to be an issue on appeal. In Zajac v. United Airlines another federal judge (in Maryland) held that the Airline Deregulation Act preempted a similar greenwashing claim tied to ticket prices.

But the strongest argument Delta has may be that the lead plaintiff testified that carbon-neutral advertising played no role in the four ticket purchases used to support her claim. An ex-boyfriend, her parents and an employer paid for some of her travel, with schedule, convenience and SkyMiles also entering her choices.

She later submitted a declaration and deposition corrections backing away from that.

The proposed class includes California residents exposed to the campaign from September 1, 2021 through March 31, 2022 who bought Delta tickets beginning September 1, 2021. Delta says 1,452,601 people with at least one California address bought a ticket between March 1, 2020 and March 31, 2022.

Delta will try to break up any class because what each customer saw depends on where they look (press releases and social posts, Delta.com rotating banners, while napkins or seatback screens reached passengers after they had bought a ticket).

Meanwhile, they have survey data showing the carbon neutral claims barely resonated – that 0.1% of survey respondents and zero in California mentioned the environment or carbon neutrality when asked why they chose an airline. What a waste! And they’ll argue they acted in good faith buying the credits, that it’s not their fault they turned out to be a sham.

Delta Probably Prevails

Delta made an absolute claim about current carbon neutrality and relied on a voluntary market with real weaknesses to deliver on the claim. Indeed, they name even say that it’s “hard-to-abate” aviation emissions and that its existing fleet, current technology and available fuel cannot deliver its long-term emissions goals.

But the plaintiff is going to have a hard time demonstrating reliance on the claims in buying tickets and paying a premium to do so. They’re going to have a hard time certifying the class. And Delta has strong Airline Deregulation Act preemption arguments for appeal.

title: Bunge to supply soybean oil for Brazil's largest renewable fuels project - Biofuels Digest
description:
Bunge to supply soybean oil for Brazil’s largest renewable fuels project In Ukraine, UkrAgroConsult reported that global agribusiness company Bunge has signed a five-year agreement with Acelen Renewables to supply 300,000 tons of certified soybean oil annually for a new biorefinery in Brazil’s Bahia state.
According to Acelen Renewables, the agreement is a key step toward securing a reliable feedstock supply chain for the future biorefinery.
The company aims to ensure long-term access to certified raw materials needed for large-scale renewable fuel production, strengthening Brazil’s position in the global low-carbon fuels market, according to the report.
Its first production unit will have the capacity to produce 1 billion liters of SAF and HVO per year, making it one of the largest renewable fuel facilities in the region.
In addition to soybean oil, the plant will use used cooking oil (UCO) and macaúba oil, derived from a native Brazilian palm, as feedstocks.
text:
Bunge to supply soybean oil for Brazil’s largest renewable fuels project

In Ukraine, UkrAgroConsult reported that global agribusiness company Bunge has signed a five-year agreement with Acelen Renewables to supply 300,000 tons of certified soybean oil annually for a new biorefinery in Brazil’s Bahia state.

The facility is scheduled to begin operations in 2029 and will become South America’s first large-scale producer of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and renewable diesel (HVO).

According to Acelen Renewables, the agreement is a key step toward securing a reliable feedstock supply chain for the future biorefinery. The company aims to ensure long-term access to certified raw materials needed for large-scale renewable fuel production, strengthening Brazil’s position in the global low-carbon fuels market, according to the report.

The biorefinery will be built at an existing industrial site in São Francisco do Conde on Brazil’s Atlantic coast. Its first production unit will have the capacity to produce 1 billion liters of SAF and HVO per year, making it one of the largest renewable fuel facilities in the region.

In addition to soybean oil, the plant will use used cooking oil (UCO) and macaúba oil, derived from a native Brazilian palm, as feedstocks.

description:

Chairing a high-level stakeholder meeting organized by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, Naidu reviewed progress in SAF production, certification, supply chain development and the country’s roadmap for meeting future blending requirements under the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) global carbon reduction framework.

text:
Turning waste into fuel

LanzaTech’s approach begins with an idea that sounds deceptively simple. “What we do is we recycle waste emissions and convert them into sustainable aviation fuel,” says Holmgren. “Ethanol is our intermediate and really it’s just a matter of taking every type of waste from rubbish to agri-residues to industrial waste like CO2 and converting that.”

The explanation captures the essence of the company’s technology. Rather than relying on conventional fossil feedstocks, LanzaTech uses carbon from waste streams to produce ethanol, which can then be converted into SAF.

From concept to commercial reality

For Holmgren, one of the clearest signs of progress is that LanzaTech’s technology has been proven in practice. “I am most proud of the fact that we have successfully built and made product out of what would be our first-of-a-kind technology,” she says.

LanzaTech can convert many types of waste into ethanol. Last year, LanzaJet, the company that LanzaTech spun out to commercialise alcohol-to-jet technology, produced fuel at the first-of-a-kind Freedom Pines Fuels plant in Soperton, Georgia. This marked the world’s first commercial-scale production of jet fuel using ethanol as a feedstock.

That technical progress has been matched by changes in the regulatory landscape. Holmgren pointed to the growing recognition of recycled carbon fuels in Europe as another significant step forward. “Recycled carbon fuels now have a full seat at the table in the UK and in the EU. Before that, you had to have something like corn or sugar. Now you can use industrial waste or rubbish.”

The commodity bet

Holmgren attributes much of LanzaTech’s strategy to an early strategic decision. While many biotechnology companies pursued high-value specialty chemicals, LanzaTech decided to focus on ethanol instead.

“What we went after was a commodity market, which is ethanol,” she explains. “Ethanol is the perfect intermediate to make sustainable aviation fuel, to make diesel, to make marine fuel, and to make materials. So by choosing a common molecule rather than an esoteric molecule, we’re able to create a platform.”

An overlooked resource

For Holmgren, one of the biggest opportunities for sustainable aviation lies in a resource that is often overlooked. “I think the use of waste feedstocks is an underrepresented lever,” she says. “I think people don’t realise how much carbon is above ground that we can use to make products. Everybody still continues to rely on carbon that’s below ground.”

The same conviction was reflected in Holmgren’s answer to the final question of the interview. Asked to complete the sentence, “The future of flying is…”, her response was immediate: “Circular. It’s made from waste resources.”

Whether recycled carbon becomes a major pillar of the SAF industry remains to be seen. For Holmgren, however, the opportunity is clear: the carbon needed to produce tomorrow’s fuels may already exist in today’s waste.

title: Kerosinezorgen voor KLM, maar de schone brandstof van de toekomst is net zo'n hoofdpijndossier
description:
Dit jaar verwacht het Frans-Nederlandse bedrijf 2 miljard euro extra te moeten betalen voor kerosine, een brandstof gemaakt van aardolie.
Nog altijd veel meer dan voor de blokkade van de Straat van Hormuz.
Wel is het gelukt om een groot deel van de extra kosten met prijsverhogingen op de klanten te verhalen.
Milieuorganisatie Natuur en Milieu deed onlangs met KLM, Schiphol en SkyNRG de oproep aan de overheid om de productie van e-Saf te versnellen.
De luchtvaart gelooft vooral in technologische oplossingen om de uitstoot te verminderen.
text:
De hoge brandstofkosten bezorgen Air France-KLM financiële tegenwind, zegt het luchtvaartconcern, oftewel: kopzorgen. Dit jaar verwacht het Frans-Nederlandse bedrijf 2 miljard euro extra te moeten betalen voor kerosine, een brandstof gemaakt van aardolie.

Door de oorlog in Iran steeg de marktprijs plotseling naar 1470 dollar per ton vliegtuigbrandstof. Over heel 2025 was dat gemiddeld 792 dollar. Olietankers konden de raffinaderijen niet bereiken en de voorraad kerosine liep snel terug, met een kerosinecrisis als gevolg.

De ontwikkelingen in het Midden-Oosten en de mogelijke gevolgen voor brandstofprijzen, luchtruimen en mondiale handelsstromen blijven moeilijk voorspelbaar, zegt KLM over de resultaten in het tweede kwartaal.

Maar moederbedrijf Air France-KLM ziet in een vooruitblik nog geen eind aan de hoge prijzen. Als de aardolieprijs de rest van het jaar onder de 90 euro blijft, zal de prijs van vliegtuigbrandstof iets terugzakken naar ruim 1200 dollar per ton, verwacht het concern. Nog altijd veel meer dan voor de blokkade van de Straat van Hormuz.

Wel is het gelukt om een groot deel van de extra kosten met prijsverhogingen op de klanten te verhalen. Mede hierdoor kwam KLM in de eerste helft van dit jaar op een klein plusje uit. De operationele winst bedroeg 68 miljoen euro op een omzet van 6,8 miljard – een winstmarge van 1 procent.

Duurzame brandstoffen zijn nog duurder

Kerosine was meestal een goedkope brandstof voor de luchtvaart. De duurzame luchtvaartbrandstoffen die ervoor in de plaats moeten komen, zijn drie tot vier keer duurder, zegt KLM-CEO Marjan Rintel in vakblad Industrielinqs. Saf, een afkorting van het Engelse sustainable aviation fuel, wordt bijvoorbeeld gemaakt van gebruikt frituurvet of dierlijke vetten uit slachtafval. Het zorgt voor een lagere CO2-uitstoot van minstens 65 procent.

Luchtvaartmaatschappijen mengen het nu al bij, omdat de Europese Unie dat verplicht. Bij vertrek vanaf een Europese luchthaven moet er ten minste 2 procent Saf in de tank zitten. Stapsgewijs moet dat oplopen naar 70 procent in 2050. Voor Air-France KLM is Saf nu een extra kostenpost van 250 miljoen euro.

Dankzij de Europese regels kunnen investeerders die Saf-fabrieken bouwen, op klanten rekenen. Op chemiepark Delfzijl is het bedrijf SkyNRG bijvoorbeeld begonnen met de bouw van een fabriek voor alternatieve vliegtuigbrandstoffen. KLM is een van de aandeelhouders en neemt na de opening in 2028 driekwart van de productie af. Dat is 2 procent van het totale brandstofverbruik van de luchtvaartmaatschappij.

Er zitten trouwens risico’s aan het gebruik van biomaterialen voor brandstof. Zo kan de productie extra ontbossing in gang zetten of de voedselteelt verdringen.

Te weinig frituurvet

Een groot probleem is dat er na 2030 een tekort aan afvaloliën en -vetten ontstaat. De vraag zal het aanbod ruimschoots gaan overtreffen. Europa haalt veel van de benodigde grondstoffen uit Azië en als de tekorten oplopen, kunnen landen zoals China en Maleisië besluiten om die zelf te houden. ‘Met frituurolie alleen komt Saf niet van de grond’, concludeert Industrielinqs in een analyse.

Het is volgens de luchtvaart dus nodig om brandstoffen te maken met een andere technologie. Zoals in fabrieken die groene waterstof, gemaakt met hernieuwbare energie, en CO2 combineren tot e-Saf. Deze duurzame brandstof kan volgens KLM-CEO Rintel wel negen tot tien keer zo duur zijn als kerosine.

Hierbij heeft de luchtvaart flinke concurrentie van andere industrieën die groene waterstof willen gebruiken, zoals kunstmestfabrieken. Staalbedrijven schatten in dat groen staal voorlopig veel te duur is. Investeerders steken nu ook nog geen geld in e-Saf-fabrieken.

Milieuorganisatie Natuur en Milieu deed onlangs met KLM, Schiphol en SkyNRG de oproep aan de overheid om de productie van e-Saf te versnellen. E-kerosine draagt bij aan de Nederlandse brandstof-autonomie en aan innovatie, schreven zij, en helpt bij het behalen van de klimaatdoelen.

Daarop kwam kritiek van burgerorganisatie SchipholWatch. E-Saf is ‘te duur, te traag, te energie‑hongerig’ en leidt af van de discussie over minder vliegen. De luchtvaart gelooft vooral in technologische oplossingen om de uitstoot te verminderen. Of die gaan werken is de vraag.

title: BPCL and Akasa Air partner to accelerate Sustainable Aviation Fuel adoption in India
description:
The MoU was signed by Sujit Kumar, Chief General Manager – Marketing (Aviation), BPCL, and Ankur Goel, Chief Financial Officer, Akasa Air, in the august presence of Subhankar Sen, Director (Marketing), BPCL, and Sanjeev Kumar, Business Head – Aviation, BPCL and other senior leaders from BPCL & Akasa Air.
Both organisations will jointly support the development of India's SAF ecosystem through knowledge sharing, policy advocacy, and engagement with government and industry stakeholders.
We have undertaken several digital transformation initiatives, including our state-of-the-art automation platform ‘Be-Winged’, to enhance customer experience and operational efficiency across the aviation fuel business.
We are actively working to develop the Sustainable Aviation Fuel ecosystem in India and are making significant investments in this area, including the development of a 61 KTPA Sustainable Aviation Fuel Facility at Mumbai Refinery.
In line with its commitment towards sustainability, BPCL is actively advancing multiple green energy initiatives, including the development of a 61 KTPA Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) facility at its Mumbai Refinery.
text:
Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), a Fortune Global 500 company and a Maharatna PSU, and Akasa Air, India's fastest-growing airline, announced the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to collaborate on advancing the adoption of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) in India. The partnership marks an important step towards strengthening the country's SAF ecosystem and supports India's broader decarbonization ambitions, while aligning with global aviation sustainability frameworks, including ICAO’s CORSIA mandate.

The MoU was signed by Sujit Kumar, Chief General Manager – Marketing (Aviation), BPCL, and Ankur Goel, Chief Financial Officer, Akasa Air, in the august presence of Subhankar Sen, Director (Marketing), BPCL, and Sanjeev Kumar, Business Head – Aviation, BPCL and other senior leaders from BPCL & Akasa Air.

The MoU will accelerate collaboration in establishing a framework for the supply and offtake of SAF-blended Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) at designated airports across India. The partnership will also focus on enabling long-term supply readiness by sharing indicative demand forecasts, supporting production planning, and working towards a phased increase in SAF blending as the domestic ecosystem matures. Both organisations will jointly support the development of India's SAF ecosystem through knowledge sharing, policy advocacy, and engagement with government and industry stakeholders.

Speaking on the occasion, Sen said: “BPCL is committed to providing comprehensive fuel solutions to the aviation sector through reliable supply, operational excellence and innovation. We have undertaken several digital transformation initiatives, including our state-of-the-art automation platform ‘Be-Winged’, to enhance customer experience and operational efficiency across the aviation fuel business. As India advances towards a low-carbon future, BPCL is actively pursuing multiple green energy initiatives and is committed to supporting the aviation industry's decarbonization journey through sustainable and innovative energy solutions.”

Kumar added: “BPCL shares a long-standing and valued relationship with Akasa Air, and this partnership marks another important milestone in our association. We are actively working to develop the Sustainable Aviation Fuel ecosystem in India and are making significant investments in this area, including the development of a 61 KTPA Sustainable Aviation Fuel Facility at Mumbai Refinery. Through collaborations such as this, BPCL aims to facilitate the availability and adoption of SAF, supporting the aviation sector's transition towards a more sustainable future.”

Commenting on the partnership, Goel, Akasa Air, said: "At Akasa Air, sustainability is one of our core values, shaping decisions we make across our business. Since inception, we have focused on building a modern, efficient airline through next-generation aircraft, technology and responsible practices on ground and in air. Our collaboration with BPCL builds on this foundation by strengthening our operational readiness for Sustainable Aviation Fuel and supporting the development of the supply ecosystem in India."

BPCL continues to play a pivotal role in meeting the evolving fuel requirements of the aviation sector through reliable supply, operational excellence, and innovative digital solutions. The company's state-of-the-art Be-Winged platform has enhanced customer experience and operational efficiency across its aviation business. In line with its commitment towards sustainability, BPCL is actively advancing multiple green energy initiatives, including the development of a 61 KTPA Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) facility at its Mumbai Refinery. Through strategic partnerships and investments, BPCL aims to support the growth of India's SAF ecosystem and contribute to the decarbonization of the aviation industry.

text:
New Delhi, India: As India prepares for the mandatory implementation of the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) from January 1, 2027, the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) has stepped up efforts to establish a robust Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) ecosystem.

Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu recently chaired a high-level stakeholder meeting to review the country’s preparedness for SAF adoption, carbon accounting mechanisms and compliance with global aviation emissions standards. The review comes as the government moves closer to finalising India’s draft Sustainable Aviation Fuel Policy, which is currently undergoing inter-ministerial consultations.

The meeting brought together senior officials from the Ministry of Civil Aviation, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), Airports Authority of India (AAI), Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs), airlines, airport operators and other key industry stakeholders. Discussions focused on ensuring that India is operationally ready before the mandatory CORSIA phase begins in 2027.

A key focus of the meeting was the progress of domestic Sustainable Aviation Fuel production. Officials reviewed the status of SAF production facilities being developed by Oil Marketing Companies, their commissioning timelines, certification processes and measures required to ensure sufficient fuel availability for airlines from 2027 onwards. Stakeholders also assessed India’s preparedness to build a reliable domestic supply chain capable of supporting growing SAF demand while reducing dependence on imported sustainable fuels.

The government also reviewed the proposed national roadmap for SAF blending, outlining the responsibilities of fuel suppliers, airlines and airport operators in implementing the programme. Discussions covered fuel production, transportation, airport storage infrastructure and distribution systems required to integrate Sustainable Aviation Fuel into regular aviation operations across the country.

Another major area of discussion was the creation of a comprehensive accounting, monitoring and reporting framework aligned with ICAO’s CORSIA requirements. Officials examined plans to establish a national SAF Registry that would provide end-to-end traceability of Sustainable Aviation Fuel throughout its production, transportation and consumption cycle. The registry is expected to support accurate emissions accounting and improve transparency in SAF certification and usage.

The meeting further reviewed India’s preparedness for implementing CORSIA-related regulatory requirements, including the issuance of Letters of Authorisation and the development of a CORSIA-compliant domestic carbon market framework. These mechanisms are intended to ensure that Indian airlines can meet international emissions reporting and offsetting obligations while maintaining compliance with ICAO standards.

According to the Ministry of Civil Aviation, significant progress has already been made in developing India’s SAF supply chain and carbon accounting systems. However, Minister Ram Mohan Naidu directed all concerned ministries, regulators and industry stakeholders to accelerate implementation so that the country is fully prepared before CORSIA enters its mandatory phase in January 2027.

The Minister also informed stakeholders that the draft Sustainable Aviation Fuel Policy is in its final stages and is being refined through consultations with multiple ministries and industry participants. The policy is expected to provide a long-term framework for domestic SAF production, blending, certification and commercial deployment while supporting India’s aviation decarbonisation goals.

Emphasising affordability, Naidu stated that passenger interests would remain central to the policy framework. The government aims to minimise the financial impact of SAF adoption on airlines and travellers by identifying the most cost-effective methods for fuel production, transportation, distribution and airport supply.

India has already outlined a phased SAF blending roadmap under its broader decarbonisation strategy, targeting a 1% blend in 2027, increasing to 2% in 2028 and reaching 5% by 2030. These targets are intended to support compliance with international emissions reduction commitments while encouraging investment in domestic SAF production capacity and associated infrastructure.

CORSIA, developed by the International Civil Aviation Organization, is the first global market-based mechanism designed to stabilize carbon dioxide emissions from international aviation. From January 1, 2027, participation enters its mandatory phase for eligible states, requiring airlines to monitor, report and offset emissions above prescribed baseline levels through approved carbon reduction measures, including the use of Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

The government’s latest review reflects India’s broader strategy of strengthening domestic SAF production, establishing transparent carbon accounting systems and creating the regulatory framework needed for seamless compliance with international aviation environmental standards. With the draft SAF policy nearing completion, the coming months are expected to focus on finalising implementation mechanisms, expanding production capacity and ensuring that the aviation sector is ready ahead of the 2027 CORSIA deadline.

text:
Tangerang, Indonesia: A Malaysian airline pilot has been arrested in Indonesia after authorities allegedly discovered more than 70,000 ecstasy pills in his luggage following a scheduled flight from Kuala Lumpur to Jakarta, in a case that has prompted a criminal investigation and an internal review by Malaysia Airlines.

Indonesian Customs announced on July 31 that the 39-year-old pilot, identified only by the initials MSBO, was arrested on July 29 at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport shortly after operating a Malaysia Airlines service from Kuala Lumpur. Authorities have not publicly released his full identity.

According to Indonesian officials, customs officers intercepted the pilot after receiving intelligence and allegedly recovered 70,114 MDMA (ecstasy) pills along with 2.7 grams of methamphetamine from his luggage. Officials said the seized MDMA weighed approximately 26 kilograms. A search of the suitcase uncovered 14 large packages of ecstasy pills and one package containing methamphetamine, police said.

Customs officials alleged that the pilot had agreed to transport the suitcase on behalf of another individual in exchange for 50,000 Malaysian ringgit (about US$12,200). Authorities described him as acting as a courier and said investigations are continuing to identify others connected to the suspected trafficking operation.

Officials further stated that a urine test allegedly returned positive results for cocaine and methamphetamine, indicating the suspect was under the influence of drugs at the time of his arrival in Jakarta.

The pilot has been formally designated a criminal suspect under Indonesian law. Authorities said investigators in Indonesia are coordinating with their Malaysian counterparts as the investigation continues.

Malaysia Airlines has declined to comment on the details of the case, citing the ongoing investigation. However, the airline said it maintains zero tolerance for any form of misconduct, has launched an internal review and will cooperate fully with the relevant authorities.

text:
Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) is moving ahead with a significant expansion of its refining infrastructure, aiming to raise its total capacity from the current 80.5 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) to 98 MTPA within the next two years. This push for added capacity comes as India works to secure reliable energy supplies amid volatile global oil markets and increasing consumption requirements. For a company that manages the largest share of India's refinery capacity, this expansion is a strategic move to ensure it can handle higher throughput as domestic demand for fuel continues to rise.

Balancing Traditional Oil and Green Transition

The company is not only focused on volume but also on changing how it processes fuel. By integrating bio-feedstocks directly into its existing refinery processes, Indian Oil aims to lower the carbon intensity of its traditional operations. This approach allows the company to leverage its existing large-scale assets while moving toward cleaner energy standards. Furthermore, the company is actively developing Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) at its Panipat refinery, having already established supply agreements with airlines such as Air India and Akasa Air. Beyond traditional refining, the company has expanded its footprint in the clean mobility space by installing 14,000 electric vehicle charging points and over 1,000 battery swapping stations across the country.

Managing Exposure to Global Price Volatility

India currently imports roughly 90% of its crude oil requirements, making the industry highly sensitive to geopolitical tensions. Recent disruptions in key shipping regions like the Strait of Hormuz have highlighted the risks to India’s import bill, where even a $1 per barrel increase in global crude prices can add approximately ₹16,000 crore annually to the national import cost. To mitigate these risks, Indian Oil has diversified its crude sourcing to about 40 different countries, reducing its reliance on any single region for its feedstock.

Investor Monitorables

While the expansion of refining capacity supports long-term growth, investors may watch how the company balances this heavy capital spending with its debt position. The ability to maintain healthy profit margins will depend on global crude price trends and the company’s ability to execute these modernization projects without significant cost overruns. Additionally, the shift toward green hydrogen and LNG as alternative mobility solutions represents a long-term capital commitment that will require monitoring of future returns on capital. Shareholders will likely look for updates on the commissioning timelines of the new refinery capacity and the profitability of the newer sustainable fuel segments in upcoming quarterly results.

title: Sustainable Aviation Fuel: India's Next Green Flight Path | SustainVerse
description:
For India, adopting Sustainable Aviation Fuel is not simply a question of replacing one fuel with another.
India is gradually bringing Sustainable Aviation Fuel into the centre of its clean energy and climate strategy.
Cost remains one of the biggest hurdles for Sustainable Aviation Fuel.
Despite these challenges, experts emphasise that Sustainable Aviation Fuel is only one part of the solution.
For India, Sustainable Aviation Fuel represents more than an alternative fuel- it offers an opportunity to reshape the future of cleaner aviation.
text:
As India pushes sustainable aviation fuel to cut aviation emissions, questions over feedstocks, costs and competition for land and food are beginning to shape the debate

Kolkata| August 1, 2026:

The future of aviation may depend not only on how aircraft are designed, but also on what powers them.

Today, aviation contributes around 2–3% of global carbon dioxide emissions, and unlike road transport, long-distance flights still have limited alternatives to conventional liquid fuels.

As governments and airlines look for ways to reduce emissions without disrupting air travel, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) has emerged as one of the sector's most promising solutions.

For India, adopting Sustainable Aviation Fuel is not simply a question of replacing one fuel with another. It requires balancing climate ambitions with economic viability, feedstock availability and long-term sustainability.

SAF is produced from renewable or waste-based feedstocks instead of conventional crude oil.

Depending on the production pathway, it can substantially reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions while remaining compatible with existing aircraft engines and airport infrastructure.

Its compatibility with existing aircraft engines and airport infrastructure makes SAF one of the most practical and scalable solutions for reducing aviation emissions.

India is gradually bringing Sustainable Aviation Fuel into the centre of its clean energy and climate strategy.

Government agencies, airlines, oil marketing companies and research institutions are working to expand domestic production, support pilot projects and prepare for future blending mandates.

Beyond reducing aviation emissions, these efforts are intended to strengthen energy security and help India secure a place in the emerging global SAF market.

The real challenge, however, extends beyond policy ambition. It lies in ensuring a sustainable and reliable supply of feedstock that can support production on a commercial scale.

Experts point to agricultural residues, used cooking oil, municipal solid waste, forestry waste and certain non-food energy crops as the most promising sources for Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

Unlike food-based feedstocks, these resources can help reduce emissions without affecting food security.

The challenge, however, lies in building efficient supply chains, as collecting, transporting and processing these materials remains expensive and operationally complex.

The conversation becomes far more complex when cleaner fuel begins to compete with food and land resources.

Using edible oils, sugar crops or fertile agricultural land as feedstocks could place additional strain on food prices, water availability and rural livelihoods.

Environmental experts also warn that clearing forests or natural ecosystems to cultivate energy crops may erode many of the climate gains that Sustainable Aviation Fuel seeks to achieve.

As a result, the real challenge is not simply producing cleaner aviation fuel- it is ensuring that the path to cleaner aviation does not create new environmental or social pressures along the way.

Cost remains one of the biggest hurdles for Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

Production volumes are still limited, supply chains are yet to mature and, as a result, SAF continues to cost significantly more than conventional jet fuel.

For airlines already operating in a highly competitive market with narrow profit margins, absorbing these additional costs will not be easy without targeted policy support and market incentives.

That is why the design of future blending mandates could determine how quickly SAF moves from ambition to widespread adoption.

Rather than imposing immediate large-scale adoption, many countries are introducing phased blending mandates that gradually expand the use of Sustainable Aviation Fuel while supporting domestic production and maintaining industry competitiveness.

Experts argue that India will need a similar approach—one that balances climate commitments with commercial realities and gives producers, refiners and airlines the certainty and time needed to expand investments, production capacity and supporting infrastructure.

Despite these challenges, experts emphasise that Sustainable Aviation Fuel is only one part of the solution.

Reducing aviation emissions will also depend on more fuel-efficient aircraft, improved air traffic management, operational efficiencies and the development of future technologies such as hydrogen-powered aircraft.

The future of aviation decarbonisation won’t rest on SAF alone. It will sit alongside efficiency, new aircraft, and operational changes.

For India, Sustainable Aviation Fuel represents more than an alternative fuel- it offers an opportunity to reshape the future of cleaner aviation.

A successful SAF ecosystem could create economic value from agricultural waste, strengthen energy security, encourage innovation and help the country move closer to its climate commitments.

But lasting success will depend on ensuring that the transition protects food security, safeguards ecosystems and supports the communities that depend on them.

The future of aviation will not be judged only by how much it reduces emissions, but by how responsibly it achieves that transition. Because sustainable flight truly begins long before it’s take-off - with fuel that is as sustainable in its production as it is in its purpose.

title: Reflect Orbital Eärendil-1 approval: The fight over space mirrors - Aerospace Global News
description:
While the approval covers a single demonstration satellite, it has already sparked a wider debate about how emerging space technologies should be regulated.
Reflect Orbital argues that orbital reflectors could make better use of existing renewable energy infrastructure.
Reflect Orbital believes sunlight from space could extend renewable energy generation The company says the idea addresses one of solar power’s biggest limitations.
Reflect Orbital argues that orbital mirrors could extend the operating hours of existing solar farms by reflecting sunlight onto them before sunrise or after sunset.
It argues that increasing the output of existing solar farms could become increasingly valuable as solar energy accounts for a growing share of electricity generation in many countries.
text:
The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has approved Eärendil-1, a demonstration satellite developed by California-based startup Reflect Orbital that is designed to reflect sunlight onto selected locations on Earth after sunset.

The decision clears the way for what would become the first spacecraft built specifically to redirect natural sunlight back to the Earth’s surface, a concept intended to extend the operating hours of solar farms and other commercial applications.

While the approval covers a single demonstration satellite, it has already sparked a wider debate about how emerging space technologies should be regulated.

Reflect Orbital argues that orbital reflectors could make better use of existing renewable energy infrastructure. Astronomers counter that deliberately illuminating the night sky raises questions that current satellite licensing frameworks were never designed to address.

The case has therefore become an early test of how regulators, scientists, and industry will balance commercial innovation with the protection of one of Earth’s shared natural resources.

Eärendil-1 differs fundamentally from the thousands of satellites already operating in low-Earth orbit

It is not designed to provide communications, navigation, or Earth observation services. Instead, the spacecraft will carry an 18-metre by 18-metre thin-film reflector intended to redirect sunlight onto selected locations while orbiting at an altitude of around 600 to 650 kilometres.

Reflect Orbital has presented the mission as a technology demonstrator for a longer-term concept that could eventually support solar power generation beyond sunset using orbital reflectors.

Reflect Orbital believes sunlight from space could extend renewable energy generation

The company says the idea addresses one of solar power’s biggest limitations.

Electricity demand in many countries reaches its highest levels during the evening, just as solar generation declines after sunset. Although battery storage has become an increasingly important part of modern electricity networks, batteries store energy rather than create additional generation capacity.

Reflect Orbital argues that orbital mirrors could extend the operating hours of existing solar farms by reflecting sunlight onto them before sunrise or after sunset. Rather than replacing batteries, the company sees the technology as complementing energy storage by allowing solar installations to continue producing electricity for longer periods using existing panels, inverters, grid connections, and land.

According to the company, extending the daily generation window could improve the utilisation of existing solar infrastructure without requiring additional ground-based construction. It argues that increasing the output of existing solar farms could become increasingly valuable as solar energy accounts for a growing share of electricity generation in many countries.

The concept represents a different approach to increasing renewable energy production.

While most investment has focused on improving photovoltaic efficiency, battery storage, or grid infrastructure, Reflect Orbital is proposing to increase the amount of usable sunlight itself by using space-based reflectors.

That proposition has attracted attention well beyond the energy sector.

Astronomers argue that reflected sunlight creates a different challenge from conventional satellites

Concerns over satellite constellations are not new.

Large communications constellations have prompted years of discussion about their impact on astronomical observations, particularly during twilight when satellites remain illuminated by the Sun.

Eärendil-1, however, represents a different category.

For conventional satellites, reflected sunlight is an unavoidable consequence of spacecraft operating in orbit. In Reflect Orbital’s case, reflecting sunlight is the primary mission.

That distinction lies at the centre of objections raised by the American Astronomical Society (AAS), which represents more than 8,500 professional astronomers across the United States.

In a petition asking the FCC to deny the application, the organisation argued that the mission is specifically designed to disrupt the natural darkness of the night sky rather than producing reflected light as an unintended side effect.

It warned that even a single reflector satellite could interfere with optical astronomy by overwhelming sensitive detectors and affecting observations of faint celestial objects.

The AAS also argued that the effects would extend beyond the intended illumination area because sunlight scattered through the Earth’s atmosphere would create a broader halo around the reflected beam.

According to the society, this could affect observations at professional observatories as well as amateur astronomy, particularly during the period between nautical and astronomical twilight when many scientific observations are conducted.

Beyond astronomy, the organisation said the proposal raised wider questions about light trespass and the potential effects of introducing artificial daylight into areas that had not chosen to receive it.

Research suggests brightness, not satellite numbers alone, is becoming the critical issue

The debate surrounding Eärendil-1 has also been shaped by new research examining how satellite constellations affect the night sky.

A recent study led by astronomer Olivier Hainaut evaluated the impact of current and proposed satellite constellations on astronomical observations, modelling not only visible satellite trails but also scattered light and changes to the natural brightness of the sky.

The study found that constellations of around 60,000 satellites would have only a negligible effect on natural sky brightness provided individual satellites remain fainter than magnitude 7 at an altitude of 550 kilometres, a level generally too dim to be seen with the naked eye.

The findings suggest that satellite brightness, rather than the number of spacecraft alone, is becoming one of the most important factors in preserving astronomical observing conditions.

Reflective satellite concepts, however, produced markedly different results.

According to the modelling, a constellation comparable to Reflect Orbital’s long-term concept of around 5,000 highly reflective satellites could increase scattered sky brightness by between 20% and 30%.

A fleet of 50,000 such spacecraft could raise background sky brightness by between 200% and 300%, substantially affecting ground-based observations. The study also found that extremely bright satellites could saturate astronomical detectors even when deployed in relatively small numbers.

The research does not assess Eärendil-1 as a standalone spacecraft. Instead, it examines how large constellations of intentionally bright satellites could influence future astronomical observations if deployed at scale.

The case exposes a regulatory question extending beyond one satellite

The Eärendil-1 application has highlighted an issue that extends beyond astronomy.

Modern satellite regulations were largely developed for spacecraft providing communications, navigation, weather forecasting and Earth observation services. Technologies designed to intentionally modify conditions on the Earth’s surface occupy a far less defined regulatory space

In its petition, the American Astronomical Society argued that the proposal should be assessed not only for its impact on astronomy but also for its potential effects on human health, ecosystems and unwanted light trespass before any wider deployment is considered. The organisation maintained that such issues should form part of the public-interest assessment required for satellite licensing.

The concerns reflect a broader challenge facing regulators as commercial space companies move into new markets that extend beyond traditional satellite services.

Companies are now developing spacecraft for in-orbit manufacturing, orbital computing, space-based solar power, pharmaceutical research and other commercial applications that were largely absent when many regulatory frameworks were established. Reflect Orbital’s proposal adds another category that is spacecraft designed to project natural sunlight onto the Earth’s surface.

As commercial activity in orbit becomes more diverse, policymakers are likely to face increasing pressure to determine which agencies should evaluate environmental and societal impacts that fall outside conventional space licensing.

A single demonstration could shape future policy

text:
Czech Republic Scores a Historic Asian Travel Triumph as Starlux Airlines Storms Into Europe With Game-Changing Prague–Taipei Luxury Flights

A big change is happening in air travel because STARLUX Airlines has started its first European route. This route is between Taipei and Prague. The STARLUX Airlines route to Prague is a deal. It is a flight from Taipei to Prague. This is part of STARLUX Airlines plan to expand in Europe. It will also help people visit Prague.

The first flight happened on 1 August 2026. Now people from the Czech Republic and Taiwan can fly directly to each others countries. This makes it easier for people on holiday, business trips, tour groups and visitors to travel between Europe and Asia.

This new route is a step for STARLUX Airlines. It is the time the airline has scheduled flights to Europe. Prague is the city in Europe that STARLUX Airlines is flying to. Now there is a flight from Václav Havel Airport Prague to Taipei. People can also connect to flights in Taipei to go to more places, in Asia.

Three Weekly Flights Are Initially Being Provided

During the opening phase, three flights per week are being operated between Prague and Taipei. Services from Prague are being scheduled every Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday. From October 2026, the frequency is set to be increased to four weekly flights, with an additional Monday departure being introduced.

A practical schedule has therefore been created for travellers seeking a nonstop journey between Central Europe and Taiwan. More flexibility is expected to be provided once the fourth weekly service is added in October. The expansion should also make the route more useful for organised tours, business itineraries, and travellers planning connections through Taipei.

Airbus A350 Aircraft Are Being Used

An Airbus A350-900 was initially deployed on the new long-haul service. From 1 September 2026, the aircraft is due to be replaced by the larger Airbus A350-1000. Capacity for 350 passengers across four travel classes will be provided by the larger aircraft.

First Class, Business Class, Premium Economy, and Economy Class are being offered. Different levels of comfort can therefore be selected according to passenger requirements and travel budgets. A First Class product is also being made available on the nonstop Taipei–Prague market by STARLUX Airlines.

On the Airbus A350-900 configuration announced before the launch, 306 passengers were accommodated across four cabin classes. Four seats were provided in First Class. Fully lie-flat seats with private doors were included in Business Class, while greater legroom, more spacious seating, and enhanced catering were provided in Premium Economy.

In Economy Class, two checked bags weighing up to 23 kilograms each were included under the baggage allowance publicised for the route. Personal entertainment screens were also installed at every seat. A selection of films and television programmes, including HBO MAX content, was made available.

Central Europe Is Being Connected More Closely With Taiwan

Prague’s position as a gateway to Central Europe is being strengthened by the direct connection. Easier access to the Czech Republic is now being offered to travellers from Taiwan, while a more convenient route to Taipei and wider Asia is being provided for passengers departing from Prague.

The service is also expected to be supported by demand connected with the growing semiconductor relationship between Taiwan and the Czech Republic. Business travel requirements are being addressed alongside leisure demand. The route has therefore been designed to serve tourists, corporate travellers, delegations, and passengers visiting friends or relatives.

More than 95,000 passengers in both directions could use the route during its first year, according to an estimate issued by Prague Airport when the service was announced. That projection reflects the expected combination of direct travel and connecting traffic.

The new route should not be viewed only as a link between two cities. Prague can be used as an arrival point for journeys across the Czech Republic and neighbouring European destinations. Taipei can similarly be used as a connecting hub for travel throughout Asia.

Wider Asian Connections Are Being Opened to Prague Travellers

Connections from Taipei are being offered to several important destinations within the STARLUX Airlines network. Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, Tokyo, Singapore, Osaka, and Hong Kong were identified by Prague Airport among the onward destinations available to passengers.

Travel from Central Europe to Northeast Asia and Southeast Asia can therefore be arranged through one transfer in Taipei. A wider selection of itineraries is being made available to tourists who previously depended on different European or Middle Eastern transfer points.

Direct services from Taipei are also operated by STARLUX Airlines to five destinations in the United States. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Ontario in California, and Phoenix are included in that network. Taipei is consequently being developed as a transfer point between Asia, North America, and Europe.

However, entry requirements remain dependent on every passenger’s nationality, destination, and transit arrangements. No visa or passport policy change has been introduced through the route launch. Required travel documents must still be checked before departure.

Taiwan Is Being Made More Accessible to Czech Travellers

Taipei is being presented to Czech travellers as a destination where traditional culture, modern city life, food, architecture, and nearby natural attractions can be experienced. Taipei 101, which rises to 508 metres and contains 101 floors, remains one of the city’s best-known landmarks. Its observation deck on the 89th floor can be reached by a lift fitted with an air-pressure compensation system.

Freedom Square and the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall can be included in cultural itineraries. Longshan Temple can also be visited by travellers interested in religious traditions and historic architecture. For outdoor experiences and panoramic city views, Elephant Mountain can be reached from the urban area.

With a nonstop flight now being operated, Taiwan can be considered more easily for city breaks, extended holidays, gastronomic travel, cultural tours, and multi-destination Asian journeys. Travel time and transfer complexity are being reduced because an intermediate airport is no longer required for passengers flying directly between Prague and Taipei.

Prague Tourism Is Being Given a New Asian Gateway

Prague has long been recognised for its historic centre, architectural heritage, cultural attractions, and riverfront scenery. Through the new route, these experiences are being made more accessible to travellers from Taiwan and other Asian markets connected through Taipei.

Charles Bridge, Prague Castle, Old Town Square, and the city’s wider collection of historic districts can now be reached through the direct service. Tourism businesses across Prague and the wider Czech Republic could be supported by additional international arrivals. Hotels, tour operators, restaurants, visitor attractions, ground transport companies, and regional destinations may all be reached by passengers using the new connection.

The route may also encourage longer journeys beyond Prague. Other destinations in the Czech Republic can be included after arrival, while cross-border travel across Central Europe can be organised through rail, coach, or connecting air services.

Premium Travel Has Been Placed at the Heart of the Route

STARLUX Airlines began operations in 2020 and has been positioned as one of Asia’s younger premium international carriers. Taiwan is currently connected by the airline with destinations in 13 countries and regions. The United States, Japan, Korea, Hong Kong, Macau, Vietnam, Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore are included in its wider international presence.

Premium cabin choices have been emphasised on the Prague service. At the same time, Economy Class and Premium Economy have been retained, allowing the route to be used by different categories of travellers.

During the inaugural month, a promotional partnership was arranged with La Mer. Passengers travelling in First Class and Business Class from Taipei to Prague between 1 and 29 August were provided with a La Mer Luxury Travel Set. Jolin Cai was also selected as an ambassador for the Prague route campaign, and a new version of Prague Square was prepared.

Sustainability Requirements Are Being Applied

Flights departing from Prague are being operated with a two per cent blend of sustainable aviation fuel. This measure is being applied in accordance with the European Union ReFuelEU Aviation initiative.

A lower-carbon aviation supply chain is also being supported through cooperation with Taiwanese energy partners and international sustainability policies. Carbon neutrality by 2050 continues to be pursued by STARLUX Airlines.

The sustainability measures do not remove the environmental effects of long-haul aviation. Nevertheless, regulatory requirements are being incorporated into the operation of the Prague service, and the use of sustainable aviation fuel is being introduced as part of the route’s operational framework.

A Significant Travel Milestone Has Been Reached

The arrival of STARLUX Airlines in Europe means more than having another flight at Prague Airport. A new direct tourism link has been created between Taiwan and the Czech Republic. Easier travel is now available more Asian connections are being added and there is competition for long-haul flights.

Three flights per week are starting now. Four flights per week are being planned for October. The bigger Airbus A350-1000 is expected to start flying from September. With these changes the route is being set up to meet both tourism needs and business travel demands.

Prague has been chosen as the carrier’s European destination. At the time Taipei has become a stronger gateway for European travelers to reach a wide range of Asian cities. A real improvement, in travel options has therefore been made for passengers traveling in both directions.
